reverse_outline.summary: Three key points: attacks use the shop as built, orders outlive the person, rules are dated data requirements
Checkout, addresses and pricing rules each expose the shop to a separate demand
Kestrel & Pine met all three: card attack, deletion request, scattered rules
Link from Part VII: new demands fall on the merchant-owned layer, not the vendor's
Each chapter extends the systems-and-owners map with a new column
Where Eva's jacket order meets security, privacy and rules
Preview of the commerce-security chapter: attacks, costs, control split
Preview of the privacy chapter: mapping customer records and separating person from transaction
Preview of the regulation chapter: turning rules into owned, dated work
Start with security, because the other lists rely on its identity-and-key owners

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

The KEY POINTS callout is evidence of p04 in the spec, not a paragraph of its own; its three points (attacks use the shop as built, order outlives the person, rules are dated data requirements) match the callout evidence declared under p04.
Summary (checkout, addresses and pricing rules each bring a separate demand) matches the hook's controlling idea.
Summary (Kestrel & Pine met all three: card attack, deletion request, scattered rules) matches.
Summary (Part VII link; the new demands fall on the merchant-owned layer, not the vendor's) matches.
Summary (each chapter extends the systems-and-owners map with a column) matches the claim; it omits the 'own controls' caveat, which is subordinate.
Summary (where Eva's order meets security, privacy and rules) matches.
Summary (security chapter: attacks, costs, control split) matches.
Summary (privacy chapter: mapping records, separating person from transaction) matches.

Summary (start with security because the other lists rely on its owners) matches the takeaway and its reason; it does not register the synthesis that each demand is answered by a list the merchant keeps, not by the vendor, which sits mid-sentence in a dense closing (see flow results).
Marked two_ideas by the outliner, but it is the house KEY POINTS format: three bullets each carrying one of the part's three supporting claims, declared as p04's evidence. Not a fault.
States P8-1, P8-2 and P8-3 in one bullet each.
Hook of the opening: three outside demands on what the shop already has.
Opening: the book's company met each demand, one per supporting claim.
Opening bridge: why the demands land on the merchant's layer and not the vendor's (thesis claim).
Thesis statement and roadmap: the map with three columns, one per supporting claim.
Opening: places the three demands on Eva's order (role in the journal spec).
Introduces the chapter that argues P8-1 (identities, keys, scripts, endpoints with owners).
Introduces the chapter that argues P8-2 (person vs transaction, request handling).
Introduces the chapter that argues P8-3 (rules as dated data requirements with an owner).
Closing: synthesis of the three lists and the reading order.
The three examples (checkout, delivery address in an export, pricing rule) are each stated with the demand they bring.

Caption says what the figure shows: the three doors need not be broken to be abused, and ties it to the first demand. (Its 'three public forms' collides with the paragraph's three demands; recorded under flow.)
Each case is tied to one demand of the hook and labelled fictional.
Part VII's finding and the end of the vendor's coverage are stated with what they imply: the accounts, keys and scripts the merchant adds are its own.
Each bullet states its claim; bullet 2 is backed by p07 and bullet 3's 'calendar row' only by p08 (recorded under known_before_new).
Caption explains the three outside things, each answered by a list with owners, and that the lists are columns of one map.
Caption names where each demand meets Eva's order.
The €2,900 cost is tied to the August attack and what it cost (fees and interrupted sales).
Nine systems and the tax-law vs request split are both explained, the latter with its consequence (person separated from transaction).
The worked calendar is named with its four areas as the chapter's example of rules turned into owned work.

results.quote: Kestrel & Pine, the fictional outdoor brand, met all three:
results.finding: The example relationship is stated, but 'all three' is meant to carry over the hook's three demands, which the hook never counts as three; Figure 1 sits between them and its caption counts a different three (payment form, login, admin) and covers only the first demand. Both flow readers misread or looked back for the referent (flowA A2, flowB B1).
'Part VII found ... Part VIII adds demands made on that layer' carries Part VII's finding forward and adds why the cases land on the merchant; both flow readers read it as the bridge.
'The response to these demands begins with...' names the problem by its referent and turns to the answer.
'Eva's jacket ... meets all three: security ..., privacy ..., and rules ...' instantiates the three columns in the declared order.

results.draft_locus: Figure 3 caption, directly before 'Chapters in this part'
results.quote: security at the checkout and the payment, regulation at the price, the order button, the product page and the refund clocks, privacy in every system her name reaches
results.finding: The declared carry-over is the three demands on Eva's order in the order security, privacy, regulation. p05's sentence does this, but the last words before the chapter list (Figure 3's caption) give security, regulation, privacy, so the order the section elaborates is contradicted at the boundary. flowA (A8) and the intro reader both noticed the mismatch; the intro reader was unsure of the chapter order because of it.
'then' marks the second chapter in sequence.
'Last,' marks the final chapter.

Opens by reading the chapters back on the opening's checkout and sums up: each demand is answered by a list the merchant keeps. The sentence is dense (see flow), but the summary relationship is expressed.

results.quote: Kestrel & Pine, the fictional outdoor brand, met all three:
results.finding: flowA describes the order as concrete to framework to roadmap, matching the declared small_to_large; flowB calls it 'general to specific, then the plan', though the sequence it lists (scenarios, instances, bridge, method, Eva, chapters) is the declared one. One reader's label disagrees; the lead runs concrete to general and then narrows again to Eva and the chapters, which supports either reading. Not corroborated.

results.quote: The first demand: a shop is three public forms, a payment form, a login and an admin
results.finding: flowA A1: 'Demand' not introduced until the Part VII paragraph ... 'Three public forms' clashes with the three threats; re-read to separate the two threes. flowB B1 reports the same: took 'all three' to mean the three forms, and the caption says 'The first demand' when the lead never numbered the demands. Both propose moving Figure 1 after the Kestrel & Pine paragraph. The order of ideas is fine; the caption wording and figure placement obscure it.

results.quote: and four rules that reached engineering through unrelated channels, one as a marketplace rejecting listings
results.finding: flowA A3: 'Hard to parse; could not tell what the marketplace-rejection channel meant.' flowB B2: 'Dense; ... took a re-read.'

results.quote: Three things reach a shop from outside, a script, a person with rights and a rule with a date
results.finding: flowA A7: the attackers have become 'a script'; naming inconsistent with 'attackers'. flowB B4: 'script' means an automated attacker here but the chapter list uses 'checkout scripts' for scripts the merchant adds: one word, two jobs.

results.quote: each demand is answered by a list the merchant keeps, not by the vendor, and the other lists rely on the first: owners of identities and keys
results.finding: flowA A11: 'Dense; re-read to get the dependency.' flowB B5: 'Re-read; three claims in one sentence; "the first" ambiguous until the colon.' The reverse outliner also missed the synthesis in this sentence. flowA adds that the reason for starting with security appears only here.

results.quote: a calendar row that names an owner
results.finding: flowA A10: 'calendar unexplained until the regulation chapter blurb.' flowB B6: 'only made sense once the "worked calendar" appeared. Minor.'

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶5 (Where we are in the order's journey)
results.quote: Eva's jacket, the order this book follows, meets all three
results.finding: flowA: 'Clear purpose, but the third listing of the same three things'; suggests folding Eva's paragraph into the Kestrel & Pine or map passage. flowB: 'fine here, though could sit elsewhere'; suggests it follow Kestrel & Pine directly so the concrete grounding comes before the abstract method. Neither lost the thread, but both independently find this unit loosely placed and both propose putting it with the Kestrel & Pine cases; the difficulty comes from the declared order, which the decision log has twice kept.
results.corroborated_by: flowB section 2 ('Where we are') and item 4

results.quote: The vendor covers its own service, checkout and defaults, not the accounts, keys and scripts the merchant adds.
results.finding: flowB B3: the page has just shown attacks coming through the checkout, so saying the vendor covers the checkout left the reader unsure who answers for the August attack. One reader only.

results.quote: It assigns controls to the merchant and provider
results.finding: flowA A9: the page said 'vendor' earlier; wondered whether 'provider' is a different party. One reader only.

results.quote: security at its checkout and payment, privacy in every system her name reaches, and rules at its price
results.finding: flowA A8: the paragraph orders security, privacy, rules; Figure 3's caption orders security, regulation, privacy; 'rules' and 'regulation' alternate. One flow reader (the intro reader noticed the same order clash, but is not a flow reader).

results.quote: personal data with who decides its use
results.finding: flowA A5: vague, probably a stand-in for 'controller'. One reader only.

results.quote: The map makes responsibilities actionable; each topic still needs its own controls.
results.finding: flowA A6: caveat arrives abruptly; re-read. One reader only.

results.quote: a calendar row that names an owner
results.finding: The regulatory calendar is on does_not_know and is first used in the KEY POINTS as 'a calendar row' with no prior mention; the page names it only in p08 ('Its worked calendar'). Both flow readers reported it as unexplained at first use.
results.corroborated_by: flowA item A10; flowB item B6

results.finding: 'Demand' is the page's organising term, but it first appears in Figure 1's caption, as 'the first demand', before the lead counts or names the demands (p03 introduces 'demands made on that layer'). Both flow readers reported this.
results.corroborated_by: flowA item A1; flowB item B1

results.finding: Card testing is glossed by use ('the checkout and login at machine speed', 'checkout attempts with stolen cards'); credential stuffing, skimming and account takeover are only named, as the spec allows; legal role is given in plain words ('who decides its use') as declared. No other term precedes the audience's knowledge.
Opens on a concrete puzzling scenario followed by real cases, a bridge and a claim; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, dawn of man or book report.

One paragraph: callback, synthesis, reading order. Not 'in conclusion', not a rephrased thesis alone, no body evidence. The dependency between the lists is stated only here, but as the reason for the takeaway, not a new subtopic.

States that each demand is answered by a merchant-kept list rather than the vendor, and that the other lists rely on the first; no chapter paragraph says this of the three together (though Figure 2's caption is close). So-what: begin with commerce-security. Clarity of the sentence is failed under flow.
'The opening's checkout takes a stolen card as it takes a real purchase' returns to p01's checkout and now says who answers for it.

The intro reader predicted security, privacy, regulation, one chapter each, and the column each adds (credentials, personal data, requirements with system, deadline and owner), matching the roadmap promise. It hedged on the order because Figure 3 lists regulation before privacy (see the chapters transition result).

Reader gave all three chapters in order with every expected element: card testing, takeover, scripts, credentials, €2,900, merchant/provider controls, recovery; records, purposes, request actions, Ghent nine systems, linked records and workflow; rule into owned work with scope, data, system, verification, deadline, and the calendar's four areas.

Reader said all three come from outside onto the merchant's layer the vendor does not cover, each answered by a list with owners, the lists are columns of one map, the map makes responsibilities actionable but each topic needs its own controls. It does not name the shop's existing things each demand uses (checkout, data copies, product data), but the expected answer's core is present.
(a) commerce-security for the overnight declined-card fees; (b) privacy-and-customer-data for the deletion request; (c) commerce-regulation for the rejected listings, each with the expected reason.
